region: Captive-bred (wild form: Trinidad, Venezuela, Guyana & northern Brazil)
description: A fancy strain whose males are covered in the "cobra" pattern: vertical, snakeskin-like rosettes and bars of black over yellow-green, continuing as heavy spotting through the delta tail. Females show only a faint echo of the pattern in the tail.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Trinidad, Venezuela, Guyana & northern Brazil)
description: Males are covered in a chain-link rosette pattern like reptile scales; in "lace" snakeskins the same fine black net continues through the dorsal fin and the broad tail.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Trinidad, Venezuela, Guyana & northern Brazil)
description: The tuxedo gene darkens the rear half of the body to near-black while the front stays pale, here set off by a blue tail. Unlike most guppy colors, the tuxedo marking shows in females as well as males.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Trinidad, Venezuela, Guyana & northern Brazil)
description: A classic show strain: the rear half of the body is black in both sexes, contrasting with a pale front and a solid red dorsal fin and delta tail.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Trinidad, Venezuela, Guyana & northern Brazil)
description: Mosaic guppies have a tail whose inner half is broken into a dark, irregular network over a lighter outer zone. In the blue form the base color is sky to royal blue and the head is darkened.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Trinidad, Venezuela, Guyana & northern Brazil)
description: Bred to resemble koi carp: a white to cream body with red on the head and gill covers (breeders call it "red ear") and a solid red tail and dorsal fin.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Trinidad, Venezuela, Guyana & northern Brazil)
description: Moscow guppies, a strain developed by Russian breeders, are solidly colored from head to tail; in the blue form the male is deep steel-blue all over with a metallic gleam on the head and shoulders.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Trinidad, Venezuela, Guyana & northern Brazil)
description: The darkest Moscow line: males are velvety black over body and fins, with a greenish-blue gleam on the head and shoulders in good light. Females are smoky grey with dark tails.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Trinidad, Venezuela, Guyana & northern Brazil)
description: Carries the "Japan blue" color factor, which lays a metallic sky-blue sheen over the rear of the male's body; this popular combination pairs it with a red delta tail.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Trinidad, Venezuela, Guyana & northern Brazil)
description: Red from snout to tail tip, including the body, with breeders selecting hard against any stray black or blue pigment. Females also carry red fins and a red-tinged body.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Trinidad, Venezuela, Guyana & northern Brazil)
description: An albino version of the full red: lacking black pigment, it has ruby-red eyes and a paler, pinkish-red body. Albinos see less well, so they do best without boisterous tankmates.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Trinidad, Venezuela, Guyana & northern Brazil)
description: Grass guppies have a large tail evenly sprinkled with small black dots, said to resemble grass seeds. In the blue form the tail is sky blue and the rear of the body carries a blue sheen.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Trinidad, Venezuela, Guyana & northern Brazil)
description: Platinum guppies carry a dense layer of reflective iridophores that makes the body and fins look pearly white to silver; full platinum lines show the sheen over the whole fish in both sexes.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Trinidad, Venezuela, Guyana & northern Brazil)
description: One of the oldest guppy tail types: both the upper and lower edges of the male's tail are drawn out into narrow swords. The shape is close to the wild type, so these males stay quick and agile.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Trinidad, Venezuela, Guyana & northern Brazil)
description: Also called elephant-ear or big-ear guppies: a recessive trait hugely enlarges the pectoral fins, which flap like ears and are often pale against the colored body. In this form the tail and dorsal are solid red.

region: Laguna de los Patos & Campoma lagoons, Sucre, NE Venezuela
description: Rediscovered by John Endler in 1975 and described as Poecilia wingei in 2005 from warm, hard, algae-rich lagoons near Cumaná. Males are tiny but intensely colored with orange, black and metallic green; the wild habitat is badly degraded, and pure strains survive mainly in aquaria.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: coastal lagoons near Cumaná, NE Venezuela)
description: A line selected for a bold, vertical black bar across the middle of the male's flank, set between orange and metallic green patches; males keep the wild-type double-sword tail.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: coastal lagoons near Cumaná, NE Venezuela)
description: Males show a row of narrow black vertical bars over an orange-and-green body, like tiger stripes, while females remain plain olive-grey.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: coastal lagoons near Cumaná, NE Venezuela)
description: Selected for a large red-orange patch on the male's throat, chest and lower flank, ahead of the usual black and metallic green markings.

region: Atlantic slope from Veracruz, Mexico to northern Belize
description: Wild platies are olive-brown with variable black tail-base markings, such as the moon and comet patterns that breeders later fixed, and live in warm, weedy backwaters and ditches. Hybrids with swordtails made it a classic laboratory model for inherited melanoma.

region: Atlantic slope of NE Mexico (southern Tamaulipas to northern Veracruz)
description: A subtropical platy of clear upland streams that tolerates cooler water than the southern platy. Wild males are highly variable, often with a yellow dorsal fin, red-orange tail and blue-flecked flanks, while females show dark zig-zag lines along the side.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Atlantic slope from Veracruz, Mexico to northern Belize)
description: The classic red platy, selected for solid orange-red to coral-red color over body and fins. Like most trade platies it carries some hybrid ancestry from other Xiphophorus.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Atlantic slope from Veracruz, Mexico to northern Belize)
description: A red platy with the wagtail pattern: jet-black fins and often dark lips against a bright red body. The wagtail gene darkens only the fins, leaving the body color untouched.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Atlantic slope from Veracruz, Mexico to northern Belize)
description: Named for the black marking at the tail base — a round spot flanked by two smaller dots that resembles a cartoon mouse's head. It is a fixed form of the dark tail-base spots seen in wild platies, here on a golden body.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Atlantic slope from Veracruz, Mexico to northern Belize)
description: A red platy carrying the tuxedo marking: a broad black area covers most of the flank behind the head, leaving the head, back edge and fins red.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Atlantic slope from Veracruz, Mexico to northern Belize)
description: A metallic strain whose iridophores give the flanks a pale silvery-blue sheen over a darker blue-grey back, with smoky, dark-edged fins.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Atlantic slope from Veracruz, Mexico to northern Belize)
description: Silvery-white to pale grey with a dense peppering of small black speckles over the body; the fins are often tinted orange.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Atlantic slope from Veracruz, Mexico to northern Belize)
description: A pale peach to cream platy marked with a red patch over the chest just behind the gills, which gives the strain its name.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Atlantic slope from Veracruz, Mexico to northern Belize)
description: A red wagtail platy carrying the hi-fin trait, which enlarges the dorsal fin into a tall, trailing black banner. The long fin is a target for fin-nipping tankmates.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Atlantic slope of NE Mexico)
description: A popular variatus strain shading from yellow at the head to red-orange over the rear body and tail, like a sunset; males usually show the deepest red in the tail.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Atlantic slope of NE Mexico)
description: Males are golden-yellow to orange with a red-orange tail and a tall yellow dorsal fin, while females are paler yellow; the strain is also widely sold in a hi-fin form.

region: Atlantic slope from Veracruz, Mexico to NW Honduras
description: Wild green swordtails live in clear, flowing streams; the male's "sword" is an extension of the lower tail rays, and females prefer males with longer swords. Older females occasionally develop male traits, long misread as a full sex change.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Atlantic slope from Veracruz, Mexico to NW Honduras)
description: The classic red swordtail, bred to a deep, velvety red over body and fins; the male's sword is red as well, often with a thin dark rim.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Atlantic slope from Veracruz, Mexico to NW Honduras)
description: A red swordtail with the wagtail pattern: all fins, including the male's long sword, are black against a bright red body.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Atlantic slope from Veracruz, Mexico to NW Honduras)
description: A red swordtail carrying the tuxedo marking: a broad black panel covers the mid- and rear flank, framed by red head, back and fins.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Atlantic slope from Veracruz, Mexico to NW Honduras)
description: A golden-yellow to orange strain whose scales are edged in deeper orange, recalling pineapple skin; males carry a yellow-orange sword with a dark rim.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Atlantic slope from Veracruz, Mexico to NW Honduras)
description: A calico-patterned strain with a white to cream body splashed with red-orange and black patches, bred to recall koi carp; no two fish are marked alike.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Atlantic slope from Veracruz, Mexico to NW Honduras)
description: Selected for heavy black pigment so the body appears velvety black with a green sheen on the flanks in good light; the male's sword is black.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Atlantic slope from Veracruz, Mexico to NW Honduras)
description: Lyretail swordtails have both edges of the tail drawn into long streamers and an enlarged, pointed dorsal fin. Lyretail males also grow an elongated gonopodium and usually cannot mate, so lines are kept through normal-finned males.

region: Río Pánuco basin, San Luis Potosí & Tamaulipas, Mexico
description: Males carry the longest sword in the genus, often longer than the body itself. It lives in clear, spring-fed streams and pools of the Pánuco basin, where dark lateral blotches help it blend with sun-dappled gravel.

region: Upland Río Pánuco tributaries, Tamaulipas & San Luis Potosí, Mexico
description: Named after Nezahualcóyotl, the 15th-century poet-king of Texcoco, this swordtail lives in cool, clear upland streams. Both sexes show a dark zig-zag midlateral stripe, and males carry a yellow sword edged in black.

region: Río Pánuco basin, Hidalgo & San Luis Potosí, Mexico
description: Males have almost no sword; instead they grow a fleshy nuchal hump ("sheepshead") and a tall dorsal fin, and show vertical bars. It hybridizes naturally with X. malinche where rivers meet, forming one of the best-studied hybrid zones in fishes.

region: Río Axtla & Río Huichihuayán (Pánuco basin), San Luis Potosí, Mexico
description: The smallest swordtail: males have at most a tiny nub of a sword and are silvery with a blue sheen and a fine dark midlateral line. It shoals in clear, flowing water and does best in a group.

region: Río Pánuco basin, Hidalgo, Querétaro & San Luis Potosí, Mexico
description: Many individuals carry large black "spotted caudal" blotches at the tail base, a pigment pattern that can turn into melanoma and is studied for that reason. Males have a moderate sword with black upper and lower edges.

region: Upper Río Usumacinta & Grijalva drainages, Chiapas (Mexico) & Guatemala
description: A robust relative of the green swordtail from fast, clear highland streams. Both sexes are greenish with reddish zig-zag lines along the flank, and males carry a long sword with black borders.

region: Río Coy (Río Pánuco basin), San Luis Potosí, Mexico
description: Males come in genetically fixed size classes: large males court with a tall dorsal fin and a short sword, while small "sneaker" males chase females instead. Males can darken their vertical bars during displays.

region: Río Soto la Marina basin, Tamaulipas, Mexico
description: A platy that bridges platies and swordtails: males grow a short, pointed spike on the lower edge of the tail. It lives in clear, warm springs and streams, and many fish carry a dark spot at the tail base.

region: Río Coatzacoalcos basin, Oaxaca & Veracruz, Mexico
description: A small southern swordtail named for the male's yellow-orange, dark-edged sword. Genetic studies indicate it arose through ancient hybridization between a platy and a swordtail, driven by female preference for sworded males.

region: Mexico to northern Central America (Atlantic & Pacific slopes)
description: Wild short-finned mollies are olive-grey with rows of small dark and orange dots and live in coastal rivers, springs and brackish lagoons. Heavy grazers, they spend much of the day rasping algae from rocks and plants.

region: Coastal SE USA (North Carolina to Texas) & NE Mexico
description: Lives in salt marshes, estuaries and coastal fresh water along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts. Dominant males raise a huge, blue-spotted sail of a dorsal fin to court females and face off rivals, while smaller males try to sneak matings.

region: Coastal Yucatán Peninsula, Mexico
description: The largest sailfin molly, from brackish coastal lagoons and cenote-fed waters of the Yucatán. Its sail carries more rays (about 18–19) than that of P. latipinna and starts further forward, and is edged in orange with rows of iridescent blue-green spots.

region: Atlantic slope from northern Mexico to Costa Rica
description: A short-finned molly of rivers, springs and lagoons. Some populations, such as those of the Cueva del Azufre, live in toxic hydrogen-sulfide springs and caves and have evolved larger heads and, in the cave form, reduced eyes and pigment.

region: Pacific slope of El Salvador & Honduras
description: Sold as the liberty molly, males show metallic blue flanks peppered with orange-red spots and a dorsal fin banded in red, black and white. Males are notably quarrelsome and nip the fins of slower fish.

region: Lower Río Grande, S Texas to NE Mexico (Tamaulipas)
description: An all-female species born of hybridization between sailfin and Atlantic mollies. Females need sperm from males of those species to trigger embryo development, but the father's genes are discarded (gynogenesis), so daughters are clones of their mother.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Mexico to northern Central America)
description: A fully melanistic line-bred molly, usually of mixed short-finned molly ancestry; its velvety black looks best in hard, warm water, and stressed fish turn blotchy. Males often show a thin orange rim on the dorsal fin.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Mexico to northern Central America)
description: A black molly whose upper and lower tail rays are drawn into long points, forming a lyre; males also grow an elongated, pointed dorsal fin.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Mexico to northern Central America)
description: Combines black and gold pigment: the head and front of the body are dusted golden-yellow, fading into black over the rear body and fins.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Mexico to northern Central America)
description: Line-bred for a shortened, curved spine that gives a round, pot-bellied body and an arched back. The shape is a skeletal deformity, so balloon mollies swim more clumsily than normal mollies.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: coastal SE USA & NE Mexico)
description: White to silver with irregular black spots like a Dalmatian dog; the amount of black varies from sparse dots to heavy marbling. Males of sailfin lines raise a tall, spotted dorsal fin.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: coastal SE USA & NE Mexico)
description: A melanistic sailfin molly: velvety black over body and fins, with dominant males raising a towering black sail during courtship and rival displays.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: coastal SE USA & NE Mexico)
description: A silvery-white sailfin molly marbled with irregular black patches over body and fins; the black tends to spread with age.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: coastal SE USA & NE Mexico)
description: Named after the orange-and-cream ice lolly: a white to cream body washed with orange over the back, head and fins, usually combined with a lyretail. Males raise an orange-tinted sail.

region: Mississippi basin & Gulf slope, USA & NE Mexico (introduced worldwide)
description: Stocked around the world to eat mosquito larvae, it has become one of the most invasive freshwater fishes, outcompeting and fin-nipping small native species. Females are far larger than males and show a dark gravid spot.

region: Atlantic slope, New Jersey to Florida & Alabama, USA (introduced worldwide)
description: Very similar to the western mosquitofish and long lumped with it; some males carry a black-spotted melanistic coat. Introduced across Europe and Australia for mosquito control, it now threatens many small native fishes.

region: SE USA: North Carolina to Florida & Louisiana
description: One of the smallest fishes in North America and, despite its name, a livebearer: a female releases one or two fry a day over a week or more (superfetation) rather than a single brood. It lives among dense vegetation in swamps and slow streams.

region: Coastal drainages of southern Brazil & Uruguay
description: A small, hardy livebearer with a single dark blotch on the mid-flank; a golden form peppered with black flecks ("reticulatus") is common in the hobby. It tolerates cool water and has been introduced to Western Australia and elsewhere.

region: Jamaica
description: Endemic to Jamaica; males are iridescent blue with black vertical bars on the rear body and a yellow-orange dorsal fin and tail edged in black. Females carry a large black gravid patch on the belly, the source of the name "melanogaster".

region: Lake Miragoâne basin, Haiti
description: From the area around Lake Miragoâne in Haiti; mature males develop a humped back, an enlarged, fan-like dorsal fin and bolder black bars as they age. A peaceful grazer that picks algae from every surface.

region: Southern Dominican Republic, Hispaniola
description: A sturdy algae grazer of Hispaniola's springs and coastal streams. Males show a bright yellow-orange dorsal fin with a black border, blue-sheened flanks and dark barring on the rear body.

region: Cuba & Isla de la Juventud
description: Lives in fresh and brackish coastal waters across Cuba. Yellowish with irregular black spots scattered along the flank; males are smaller with black-and-orange markings in the dorsal fin.

region: Cuba
description: Females are silvery with a metallic sheen and fine vertical bars; males are much smaller, and in many lines have a black throat and belly running back to the long gonopodium. It lives in weedy streams and ditches across Cuba.

region: Cuba
description: Named for the golden-yellow belly and lower flanks; males are much smaller than females and carry a very long, hooked gonopodium. A peaceful livebearer of Cuban streams and ponds.

region: Central Panama (Canal-zone streams, both slopes)
description: A lively, somewhat aggressive livebearer of clear forest streams; populations living with predators mature earlier and produce more, smaller young than those in predator-free headwaters. Males show orange, black-edged fins and a blue-gold sheen.

region: Pacific slope of Costa Rica & western Panama
description: A larger, predatory Brachyrhaphis of lowland streams that readily eats small fish and fry. Males have orange-tinted dorsal and tail fins with dark margins.

region: Coastal NE South America (Venezuela to Brazil) & Trinidad
description: Lives in coastal swamps and brackish ditches. Males are red-orange with black blotches and pale blue spots and a black-edged dorsal fin, while the plain grey females carry a dark spot in the dorsal fin. Formerly Poecilia picta.

region: Coastal Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana & northern Brazil
description: Males occur in several genetically fixed color morphs within the same population: plain "immaculata", blue-barred "parae", and red or yellow "melanzona" with a bold black lateral stripe (shown here). Sensitive and rarely kept outside specialist circles.

region: Southern Mexico to Honduras (Atlantic & Pacific slopes)
description: Named for the row of round black spots along the flank, like portholes. A slender, hardy livebearer of rivers and lagoons that carries embryos at several stages at once and gives birth to small broods every few days.

region: Atlantic slope of Nicaragua, Costa Rica & Panama
description: Named for the sharp keel of enlarged scales along the underside of the tail, which gives the rear body a blade-like edge. A shy, fast stream fish with a translucent amber body, blue iridescence and a yellow-orange tail.

region: Atlantic slope from southern Mexico to Costa Rica (introduced in Florida)
description: The largest poeciliid: a pike-shaped ambush predator with long, toothed jaws that hangs among plants near the surface and darts at small fish. Females are much bigger than males, cannibalistic, and give birth to large fry that hunt from day one.

region: Río Coatzacoalcos basin, Oaxaca & Veracruz, Mexico
description: Named for its brilliant turquoise-blue iris, it is a slender, active shoaler of clear forest streams. Easily startled, it jumps readily and needs a covered tank.

region: Atlantic slope of Guatemala & Honduras
description: Females are pale olive with thin dark vertical bars; males are much smaller, with a very long gonopodium and a black-edged dorsal fin. A peaceful livebearer of slow, weedy waters.

region: Atlantic slope of southern Mexico to Nicaragua
description: A robust, predatory livebearer named for the dark spots on the shoulder and at the tail base; large females readily eat any fish that fits their mouth. Formerly classified as Heterandria bimaculata.

region: Río Ameca basin near Teuchitlán, Jalisco, Mexico
description: Males flash iridescent flanks and a tail with a broad yellow outer band bordered in black; young are nourished in the womb through ribbon-like trophotaeniae and born large. Endangered in its tiny native range, it survives largely thanks to aquarium populations.

region: Río Grande de Santiago basin & Pacific drainages, Nayarit & Jalisco, Mexico
description: Mature males develop a high, arched back, a steel-blue sheen on the front of the body and a vivid orange-red tail base. Like all goodeids it bears a few large young nourished through trophotaeniae, and it is a notorious fin-nipper.

region: Upper Río Mezquital basin, Durango, Mexico
description: From spring-fed pools around Durango; males are golden-olive with a red-orange belly and black-edged red fins, while females are plainer with a row of dark blotches along the side. Endangered in the wild and kept mainly by goodeid conservation keepers.

region: Springs of the upper Río Mezquital basin near Durango, Mexico
description: Known from only a handful of springs near Durango, it is among the most endangered goodeids. Males are darker and bolder than those of the rainbow goodeid, with largely black fins.

region: Río Balsas basin, Michoacán, Guerrero & Morelos, Mexico
description: A stream-dwelling goodeid that scrapes algae and small invertebrates from stones in flowing water. Males are golden-olive with a bluish sheen and yellowish, dark-edged fins.

region: Upper Río Lerma basin, State of Mexico & Michoacán, Mexico
description: A high-altitude goodeid of cool lakes and springs above 2,000 m. Males display enormous, many-rayed dorsal and anal fins with a black border and an orange-yellow inner band.

region: Valley of Mexico (relict ponds such as Chapultepec, Mexico City)
description: Once common in the lakes of the Valley of Mexico, it now survives in a few urban ponds, notably in Chapultepec Park, and in captive conservation programs. Males are dark with large, black-bordered dorsal and anal fins.

region: Upper Río Lerma & Lake Chapala basins, Michoacán & Jalisco, Mexico
description: Males are deep-bodied and heavily blotched with black on a golden-olive background, the black increasing with age until some look almost entirely dark; females are plain with faint spots.

region: Río Teuchitlán, Jalisco, Mexico
description: Considered extinct in the wild since the 1990s, it survives in aquaria and conservation programs. Males are golden with a high, arched back and dusky fins, and are much deeper-bodied than females.

region: Upper Río Lerma basin, Michoacán & Jalisco, Mexico
description: Males show bold dark bars and blotches over a yellow-gold body, which earned the "bumblebee" name; coloration differs strongly between the isolated populations. Endangered by the loss of its spring-fed habitats.

region: Lake Chapala basin, Jalisco & Michoacán, Mexico
description: From Lake Chapala and its tributaries; silvery-olive with irregular dark bars and spots along the flank. Males develop yellowish fins and a more intense sheen in breeding condition.

region: Springs near Tocumbo, Michoacán, Mexico
description: Restricted to a few spring-fed waters in Michoacán; both sexes are covered in round dark spots on a silvery-gold body, and males have yellow-tinged fins.

region: Río Teuchitlán, Jalisco, Mexico
description: After vanishing from the wild around 2000, it was reintroduced to its native spring at Teuchitlán from aquarium-bred stock and has re-established, one of the first such comebacks for a Mexican fish. Males have a broad orange band along the tail edge.

region: Río Lerma basin incl. Lake Cuitzeo, Michoacán & Guanajuato, Mexico
description: Males are dark olive with a vivid red-orange band edging the dorsal, anal and tail fins, the "picotee" trim that gives the fish its name. Females are plainer, spotted grey-olive.

region: Estuaries & mangroves of northern South America (Venezuela to the Amazon delta) & Trinidad
description: Cruises at the surface with its bulging eyes half out of the water; each eye is split by a band of tissue into upper and lower pupils, giving simultaneous vision in air and water. It gives birth to large live young, and males' gonopodia bend either left or right.

region: Pacific coast from southern Mexico to Nicaragua
description: The Pacific counterpart of the four-eyed fish, living in estuaries and coastal lagoons where it forages for insects at the surface and for small crustaceans on exposed mudflats. Like its relative, each eye has separate aerial and aquatic pupils.

region: Southern Brazil, Uruguay & northern Argentina
description: A relative of the four-eyed fishes: the male's tubular gonopodium bends to one side and the female's genital opening is matched to one side, so "left" males pair with "right" females. Hardy and cool-tolerant, it lives in fresh and brackish coastal waters.

region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java & Borneo
description: Hangs just under the surface, snapping up fallen insects with its short upper jaw and long, fixed lower jaw. Rival males settle disputes by locking jaws and "wrestling", and were once matched in staged fights in Thailand.

region: Karst streams of the Maros region, southern Sulawesi, Indonesia
description: Males have a short, fleshy lower-jaw flap that hangs downward and red fins tipped in black. Fry are born large — nearly 2 cm — and the species roams mid-water more than other halfbeaks.

region: Southern Thailand, Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo
description: A slender blackwater halfbeak with a very long, thin lower jaw bearing a small fleshy "beard", and a long-based dorsal fin edged orange-red in males. It lives in tea-colored peat-swamp and forest streams and bears live young.

region: Coastal plains of central Mozambique (Beira region)
description: An annual killifish of rain-filled pools that hatches, matures and spawns within a single wet season; its eggs survive the dry season buried in the mud. Males are electric blue with vertical red-orange marks and a fiery, black-edged tail.

region: Southern Mozambique
description: Long confused with N. rachovii, it replaces that species in southern Mozambique's seasonal floodplain pools, where its eggs survive the dry season buried in the mud. Males are blue with bold red-orange vertical marks and a red tail with a black border.

region: SE Zimbabwe & southern Mozambique
description: The shortest-lived vertebrate kept in captivity: some strains live only 4–6 months, making it a laboratory model for the biology of aging. Males come in red-tailed (shown) and yellow-tailed forms; the widely used lab strain "GRZ" was collected in Gonarezhou National Park, Zimbabwe.

region: Coastal Tanzania & Zanzibar
description: A classic, hardy annual killifish from temporary pools of the Tanzanian coast and Zanzibar, whose eggs survive the dry season buried in the mud. Males are turquoise-green with red scale edges and a red tail bordered in black.

region: Mafia Island, Tanzania
description: Known from Mafia Island off the Tanzanian coast, where it lives in rain-filled pools. Aquarium strains include a red form, with a deep red body speckled pale blue, and a yellow-finned form; this is the red form.

region: Rufiji River floodplain, Tanzania
description: A small annual killifish from the Rufiji floodplain known in two striking male forms: an almost entirely red morph (shown) and a blue morph with red scale edging.

region: Coastal Kenya & NE Tanzania
description: From temporary pools on the East African coast, where its eggs survive the dry season buried in the mud. Males have pale blue-white flanks with a net of red scale edges, red fins and a plain red tail.

region: Coastal lowlands of Tanzania
description: Named for the male's bright red fins, which contrast with a blue-green body netted in red. It inhabits seasonal pools in the coastal lowlands of Tanzania, and its eggs survive the dry season buried in the mud.

region: Southern Mozambique, Malawi, Zimbabwe & NE South Africa
description: A large, robust, straight-backed Nothobranchius of seasonal pans; males are red-brown with blue-white scale centres and a red tail. One of the largest Nothobranchius, it needs more room than its relatives.

region: Lower Jubba & Tana river plains, Somalia & Kenya
description: Named after the ichthyologist Rex Jubb, it lives in temporary pools of the dry lowlands of Somalia and eastern Kenya, where its eggs survive the dry season buried in the mud. Males occur in red and blue forms; this is the blue form, netted with red.

region: Lake Chilwa & Lake Chiuta basins, southern Malawi
description: Restricted to seasonal pools and swamps around Lake Chilwa in southern Malawi, where its eggs survive the dry season buried in the mud. Males are blue with red scale edges and a red tail with a dark border.

region: Lower Río Paraná & Río Uruguay basins, Argentina & Uruguay
description: Males are velvety blue-black studded with tiny pearly blue-green spots and have dark fins. They live in seasonal pools of the Paraná–Uruguay lowlands, where pairs dive headfirst into the mud to spawn.

region: Lower Río Paraná & Río de la Plata basins, Argentina & Uruguay
description: The classic "Argentine pearl": males are slate-blue with faint vertical bars and rows of pale pearly spots. Pairs dive together into the soft bottom to lay eggs that must survive months of drought.

region: Río Uruguay basin, Argentina, Uruguay & southern Brazil
description: Males show blue-green flanks crossed by dark vertical bars and dotted with pale spots, with blue-spotted fins. Like other Austrolebias it lives in cool seasonal pools and spawns by diving into soft mud.

region: Coastal lowlands of Rio Grande do Sul (Brazil) & Uruguay
description: Males are boldly banded with dark vertical bars over iridescent blue-green, giving the species its common name. Its coastal seasonal pools are increasingly lost to rice farming and urban growth.

region: Coastal lowlands of Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil
description: An annual killifish of seasonal coastal pools near Rio de Janeiro, now threatened by urban expansion. Males have red-brown flanks studded with iridescent pale spots and long, flowing dorsal and anal fins.

region: Coastal swamps of Gabon around Cape Lopez
description: From shaded coastal swamps and creeks of Gabon; males are chestnut-brown speckled with crimson and have a lyre-shaped tail ending in white-tipped streamers with orange and dark bands. Eggs are laid in fine plants or spawning mops and hatch after about two weeks.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: coastal swamps of Gabon)
description: A long-established aquarium strain lacking most dark pigment: the body is golden-orange with crimson dots, while the lyre tail keeps its orange and white streamers.

region: Northern Gabon & Equatorial Guinea
description: Males are blue-green with about five rows of red dots that merge into bold horizontal stripes, carried on into a tail with red bars and yellow edges. It lives in small, shaded rainforest streams.

region: Coastal lowlands of Cameroon & SE Nigeria
description: Named for two dark horizontal bands along the flank. Males are orange-brown with large, colorful fins and a tail with extended upper and lower rays; a member of the Chromaphyosemion group of coastal rainforest streams.

region: Central Congo basin: DR Congo, Republic of Congo & Central African Republic
description: A forest-stream killifish of the central Congo basin. Males are steel-blue scattered with crimson spots, with red-banded fins edged pale and a tail whose corners are drawn into short points.

region: Lower Congo basin around Kinshasa, DR Congo
description: Males are pale sky-blue densely sprinkled with red dots that continue into all the fins. It inhabits swampy forest streams of the lower Congo around Kinshasa.

region: Coastal SE Nigeria, Cameroon & Equatorial Guinea
description: Type species of the "calliurum group" (the name means "beautiful tail"): males are blue-green with red dots and a rounded tail banded red with a yellow rim.

region: Coastal Cameroon & Equatorial Guinea
description: Named after the German ichthyologist Ernst Ahl; males are blue to blue-green with red speckling and red-banded, yellow-edged fins. A close relative of A. calliurum from coastal forest streams.

region: Southern Cameroon & northern Gabon
description: A small, slender species of shallow forest brooks (exiguum means "small"); males are yellow to amber with rows of red spots and red-banded fins with drawn-out tail corners.

region: Southern Gabon & Republic of Congo
description: Named for its "heavenly" sky-blue males, which are marked with fine red spots and have red-banded fins. It lives in small streams of the forest–savanna mosaic.

region: Coastal Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea & Gabon
description: The name means "splendid flank": males have iridescent blue-green sides with red spots and short red streaks, and red-banded fins. A coastal lowland species of small forest streams.

region: Coastal Gabon
description: Several subspecies are kept (gabunense, boehmi, marginatum) that differ in the red patterning; males have blue-green flanks dotted red and a rounded tail with red and yellow bands.

region: Southern Cameroon, Gabon & Equatorial Guinea
description: Widespread and very variable in forest streams of southern Cameroon and neighbouring countries; males show iridescent blue flanks with red spots and rows of red dots in the fins.

region: Coastal swamps of Sierra Leone
description: A large, semi-annual killifish of seasonal swamps whose eggs rest in damp peat for months before hatching. Males are golden-orange with rows of red spots and red-edged fins; formerly known as Aphyosemion occidentale.

region: Nigeria & western Cameroon
description: One of the hardiest and most popular killifish, kept in many named wild populations such as "Jos Plateau", "Lafia" and "Akure". Males are steel-blue covered in red spots, with red-spotted fins edged yellow or orange.

region: Coastal swamps of the Niger delta (Nigeria) & western Cameroon
description: A large killifish of coastal swamps, whose eggs are buried in the bottom and develop for weeks before hatching. Males are blue-green with a red-brown rear body and a three-pointed tail striped red, yellow and blue; adults readily eat small fish.

region: Coastal Nigeria, Benin & Togo
description: A semi-annual species of temporary coastal swamps whose eggs rest in damp substrate. Males are blue-green with red markings and grow long filaments from the anal fin and the corners of the tail.

region: Cross River basin, SE Nigeria
description: Named after the Danish killifish researcher Jørgen Scheel. Males are iridescent blue-green with rows of red spots and red-banded fins with pale edges; it lives in rainforest streams of the Cross River basin.

region: Sanaga River basin, coastal Cameroon
description: Named after the Swiss biologist Jean-Louis Amiet. Males are orange-red with blue-green iridescent scales on the flanks and a tail with orange-red upper and lower extensions.

region: Coastal Ghana & eastern Ivory Coast
description: A West African species of shallow forest and savanna streams that may dry out seasonally; its eggs survive in damp substrate. Males are blue-green densely spotted with red and have a yellow-rimmed tail with red bars.

region: Coastal Liberia, Ivory Coast & Ghana
description: A surface-dwelling panchax with five or six dark vertical bars on a brassy body; males of the popular "monroviae" form have a bright red-orange throat. It hangs still under floating plants to ambush insects that fall on the water.

region: Coastal West Africa from Togo to Gabon
description: A larger panchax of slow coastal streams and swamps; six dark vertical bars cross the olive-golden body, and males carry red spots and yellow-edged fins. It eats any fish small enough to swallow.

region: Upper Guinea highlands: Liberia, Guinea & Ivory Coast (Mt Nimba area)
description: One of the most colorful Epiplatys: males show rows of red spots over a bluish body and red-edged, yellowish fins. It lives in cool, clear forest streams of the Mount Nimba region.

region: Coastal Guinea, Sierra Leone & Liberia
description: A tiny surface killifish banded cream and black like a clown, the male with a "rocket flame" tail streaked red, yellow and electric blue. It lives among plants in shallow swamps and forest pools, picking tiny insects from the surface.

region: Peninsular India
description: A large surface killifish that hovers under floating plants with its flat back at the waterline, waiting for insects and small fish. Males are golden-green with rows of iridescent spots and red-dotted, yellow-edged fins; females show dark bars on the rear body.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: peninsular India)
description: A xanthic aquarium strain of the striped panchax: bright golden-yellow with rows of reflective spots and orange-red-edged fins. Like the wild form, it eats any fish small enough to swallow.

region: India & Sri Lanka to Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia & Indonesia
description: Widespread from India to Indonesia in ditches, paddies and brackish coastal waters; bluish to brownish with a dark blotch at the base of the dorsal fin and an orange-edged tail. Hardy and adaptable, it hunts insects at the surface.

region: Coastal western & southern India
description: The smallest Aplocheilus: greenish-gold with rows of shining spots and red markings in the fins. It lives in shallow pools, paddies and ditches, staying just under the surface among plants.

region: Lowland wet zone of Sri Lanka
description: Endemic to Sri Lanka's lowland wet zone, where it lives in shaded streams and marshy pools. Males are greenish-gold with rows of bright blue-green scales and fine red dots.

region: Seychelles
description: A hardy panchax from the Seychelles that tolerates brackish water. In breeding condition the male's scales stand slightly out from the body, giving a ruffled look; its golden-green body is covered in rows of red dots.

region: West & Central Africa: Senegal to Lake Chad & Cameroon
description: Named for the brilliant blue-green iridescent patch in the upper half of each eye, which shines like a lamp in dim light. Peaceful and best kept in a group, it spawns among fine plants and roots.

region: Coastal West Africa from Senegal to Angola
description: Lives in mangrove creeks, coastal lagoons and lower river courses and tolerates, even prefers, slightly brackish water. Males show shining silver-blue vertical bars on the rear body and yellowish fins.

region: Forest streams of western Cameroon & SE Nigeria
description: A lampeye of clear, flowing forest streams; unusually, it lays its eggs deep in narrow crevices of wood and rock rather than among plants. Males are iridescent sky-blue with orange-edged fins.

region: Lake Tanganyika (endemic)
description: The largest of the lampeye killifishes, endemic to Lake Tanganyika, where it forms big schools along rocky shores and lays its eggs deep in rock crevices. Its blue-green body is studded with rows of shining pearly scales.

region: Western Cuba
description: A slim, cylindrical killifish of western Cuban streams that rests just below the surface and will jump across damp leaves and banks. Males are brownish-green with rows of red dots and an orange-edged tail; females carry a dark "rivulus spot" on the upper tail base.

region: Trinidad & Tobago and coastal Venezuela & Colombia
description: Famous from the guppy streams of Trinidad, where it is often the only fish living above waterfalls; it can wriggle overland on wet nights to reach new pools. Olive to bluish with rows of red dots, it preys on young guppies.

region: Lower Amazon basin, Brazil
description: Named "tail-eye" for the dark ocellus females carry on the upper tail base. Males are green to blue-green with rows of red dots; like other rivulines it lurks near the surface and jumps well.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: lower Amazon basin, Brazil)
description: A xanthic aquarium strain that is far more widespread in the hobby than the green wild form: golden-yellow with rows of red dots and an orange-edged tail.

region: Mangroves of Florida, the Bahamas, Caribbean & Gulf of Mexico
description: The only vertebrate known to routinely fertilize its own eggs: most individuals are hermaphrodites that produce clonal offspring. It can survive for weeks out of water in damp logs and crab burrows, breathing through its skin.

region: Atlantic coast of North America: Gulf of St Lawrence to NE Florida
description: An extremely hardy salt-marsh fish that tolerates large swings in temperature, salinity and oxygen. Spawning peaks on spring high tides, and the eggs develop out of the water in empty mussel shells and marsh grass until the next high tide.

region: SE USA coastal plain: South Carolina to Texas
description: A topminnow of swamps, ponds and vegetated backwaters; males are olive-gold with rows of red-brown dots and scattered gold flecks on the flanks. It cruises just below the surface picking off insects.

region: NE North America: Atlantic slope & Great Lakes basin
description: A slender, shoaling killifish of clear, weedy lake shallows and slow rivers, with many narrow dark bars across its silvery-olive flanks. Cold-hardy, it does not need a heater.

region: Mississippi basin & Gulf slope, central & southern USA
description: Patrols the surface of quiet streams and backwaters, showing a bold black stripe from snout to tail and a gleaming pale spot on top of the head, as in other topminnows.

region: Florida & southern Georgia, USA
description: Lives in clear, vegetated springs and streams; males have an electric-blue dorsal and anal fin with a dark base and a red-orange tail base, while a dark zig-zag stripe runs along the body in both sexes.

region: Atlantic & Gulf coasts of the USA & NE Mexico
description: A small, very tolerant killifish of coastal marshes and estuaries that also lives in inland saline springs. Its scales are outlined in dark like crosshatching, and breeding males show a dark spot at the front of the dorsal fin and orange-yellow fins.

region: Atlantic & Gulf coasts from Massachusetts to Mexico & the Caribbean
description: A deep-bodied pupfish of salt marshes and lagoons that tolerates anything from fresh water to more than twice seawater salinity. Breeding males turn steel-blue on the nape with a salmon-orange belly and defend small spawning territories.

region: Lower Colorado River basin & Salton Sea area: California, Arizona & Sonora
description: Survives in desert springs, marshes and pools that can exceed 40 °C and be saltier than the sea. Breeding males turn iridescent blue with a yellow-orange tail; the species is federally endangered and kept in refuge ponds and aquaria.

region: Florida peninsula, USA
description: Named for the male's rows of red and silvery-blue lines, said to recall the US flag, it is one of the few fish that readily eats hair and thread algae. Males guard the eggs in a shallow pit or among plants until they hatch.

region: Coastal lagoons & pools of the Yucatán Peninsula, Mexico
description: A small relative of the American flagfish from coastal lagoons and pools of the Yucatán, rarely kept outside killifish societies. Like the flagfish it grazes algae, and males defend small spawning territories.

region: Coastal lagoons & salt marshes of the central & eastern Mediterranean
description: Lives in coastal lagoons, salt pans and marshes around the Mediterranean, tolerating salinities from fresh water to well above seawater. Males have bold dark vertical bars on a silvery-blue body and yellow-orange fins.

region: Red Sea, Persian Gulf & Arabian coasts; inland springs of the Middle East
description: Formerly Aphanius dispar; it ranges from fresh desert springs to hypersaline lagoons and even shallow coastal waters of the Red Sea. Males are silvery-blue with yellow fins and dark bands across the tail.

region: Coastal spring-fed wetlands of eastern Spain (Valencia & Catalonia)
description: Known locally as the samaruc, it survives in a few spring-fed coastal wetlands of eastern Spain and is critically endangered, with captive breeding supporting reintroductions. Males show a dark spot behind the gill cover and faint vertical bars.

region: Japan (southern & western Honshu, Shikoku & Kyushu)
description: A rice-paddy fish of Japan and a classic laboratory model with transparent embryos; in 1994 it became the first vertebrate to mate and spawn in orbit. Females carry the fertilized eggs in a cluster at the vent for hours before brushing them onto plants.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Japan)
description: The classic orange-yellow medaka, kept in Japan since at least the Edo period and widely sold as a pond and classroom fish. It lacks black body pigment, so the yellow-orange shows through.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Japan)
description: A strain lacking both black and yellow body pigment, leaving a milky white to pinkish body with dark eyes; it glows in shaded ponds and bowls.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Japan)
description: Lacks yellow pigment, so the remaining black pigment and reflective cells give a cool, pale silver-blue body; a traditional Japanese strain.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Japan)
description: A deep red-orange Japanese strain named after the Tang-dynasty beauty Yang Guifei (Yōkihi in Japanese); its color intensifies in sunlight and against dark backgrounds.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Japan)
description: Carries the "miyuki" trait: a band of bright metallic iridophores along the back that shines silver-blue when seen from above, the traditional way of viewing medaka in ceramic bowls.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Japan)
description: Bred to show red-orange patches on a white body like kohaku koi; the size and placement of the patches differ from fish to fish.

region: Muna Island, SE Sulawesi, Indonesia
description: Described in 2010 from shaded forest streams on Muna Island off Sulawesi and named after the Indonesian biologist Daisy Wowor. Males have a metallic blue-green upper body and a red-orange throat, belly and fin edges.

region: Mangroves & coastal waters of Java, the Malay Peninsula, Thailand & Borneo
description: A brackish-water ricefish of mangrove creeks and estuaries, almost transparent with a bright blue-green iris. It has been developed as a test species for marine pollution studies in Southeast Asia.

region: Southern Sulawesi, Indonesia
description: A ricefish of streams, ponds and paddies of southern Sulawesi; translucent olive-grey with a dark line along the rear of the body. Males develop enlarged dorsal and anal fins.
